title: Japan's Household Spending Fell 6.8% in September
paragraphs: Household spending in Japan fell by 6.8% in September compared to one year earlier, according to government data. It was the 10th month in a row that household spending declined.
The size of the drop surprised experts, who had predicted a 3% fall. The decline in spending was the biggest since 2020, when spending fell because of the coronavirus pandemic.
However, real wages — the value of people's salaries adjusted for inflation — went up by 2.2% in September compared to one year earlier.
"Since wages are rising, it's hard to explain why consumer spending isn't picking up," Takeshi Minami of the Norinchukin Research Institute told Bloomberg.

The government blamed bad weather, such as heavy rains and typhoons, for the fall in spending, because the weather stopped people from going out. In Tokyo, it rained every single day during the month of September — the first time this has ever happened.

Spending on dining out actually increased by 2.3%, possibly because there was a five-day holiday in September. But spending on food and drink fell by 2.5% as the cost of a 5-kilogram bag of rice fell below 3,000 yen — about $19 — for the first time since 2024.
The Bank of Japan will have to consider this fall in spending carefully as it decides whether or not to continue raising interest rates.

Higher interest rates should help lower inflation and bring prices down, but they also make borrowing more expensive, which can impact households taking out mortgages and loans. They also encourage people to save money rather than spend it.

The Bank of Japan has been slowly raising its interest rate to fight inflation since 2024. In September, it rose to 1.25%, the highest rate since 1995, and it's expected to rise again in the middle of December.
